content:
Here is some information supplied by the email account provider:

When creating a new folder, the server shows error: "{imaps} Bad flag in APPEND command: Nonjunk"

The error is clear — the IMAP server is rejecting the APPEND command because Thunderbird is sending two junk-related flags simultaneously:

$notjunk — a valid IMAP keyword flag NonJunk — a non-standard flag (no backslash prefix) that the server doesn't accept

This is a Thunderbird-side behavior — it's sending both $notjunk and NonJunk together when moving messages to newly created folders, and the server's IMAP parser rejects NonJunk as invalid.

Incoming Server Type: IMAP Mail Server Incoming Server Name: imap.gmail.com Port: 993 User Name: <my email address> Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: OAuth2

(if you're set up as a POP account, use these settings:)

Incoming Server Type: POP Mail Server Incoming Server Name: pop.gmail.com Port: 995 User Name: <my email address> Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: OAuth2


If these are correct, you may need to re-authenticate, which Google forces us all to do every once in a while. To do that,

- Make sure cookies are allowed (see <settings | privacy & security web content accept cookies from sites) - delete existing gmail (see <settings sites show cookies) any stored password entries <settings saved passwords>. < p></settings>

(the first step is the most important one - the others may not be necessary.)

Don't discount that Bitdefender isn't the problem. You should test it by creating an exception for Thunderbird, or, better yet, by temporarily disabling Bitdefender while you try to send a message. If you're using Windows, you can re-start in Safe Mode with Networking to do this.

content:
This just means that a spammer has gotten hold of your email address and is sending out spam impersonating you. Unfortunately, there is nothing you can do about it. It's not originating from you.

Often or usually the "From:" address shows your real name but a patently wrong address. Of course, many recipients just see your name and gloss over the address. Nothing you can do about that either, except to alert your contacts to be skeptical about such messages and to not respond to them or click any links in them. Once you learn to recognize the obvious signs they're pretty easy to recognize.

I get similar messages almost every day that purport to be from my family, usually saying something like, "I forgot to send you these pictures" and providing a link to a probably malware site. I just mark them as Spam and move on.

content:
The answer is, "No." Yahoo, Gmail, and many other email providers authenticate you using OAuth2. What happens is when Thunderbird first contacts Yahoo to send or receive email, it will ask for your Yahoo password. It will then set what's known as a "token" in your Saved Passwords, which appears as a seemingly-arbitrary string of characters and is NOT your actual password. The token indicates that you have been verified as you on that particular machine with your correct password. This is considered to be far more secure than the old plain password authentication method.

According to this article, AT&T also uses OAuth, but I have no personal experience with it:

https://www.att.com/support/article/email-support/KM1240462/

Here's an article that describes OAuth2 in good detail:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/tb-oauth

content:
No. You use your regular password everywhere, both with webmail AND in Thunderbird, when prompted. The difference is that Thunderbird won't store your password on your computer, but instead it will store a record (the token) of having authenticated you. Remember that the token is not a password, per se, and you will never need to know it.

But if you DO decide to change your password on AT&T or Yahoo, you may need to delete the tokens saved in Thunderbird's Saved Passwords, after which you will be prompted to authenticate anew... with your new password. Once you're authenticated, a brand new token will be set.

content:
Denise, you can reduce the new message indications (I'm used to calling them "badges") by unsubscribing to gmail's All Mail folder. It is a common suggestion on this forum because All Mail doubles storage requirements and causes some inefficiency. Right click on the account name in the folder pane, select "Subscribe", and uncheck "All Mail" in the list.

Another improvement might be to use different folder layouts and/or a different folder structure. The main purpose of unified folders is to show all inboxes in a single, collapsed folder. If you did that, one more badge in your first screen shot would no longer appear. But you seem to use sub-folders of the inbox, so you must expand the unified inbox to see the subfolders. As far as I know, that defeats the purpose of the unified inbox. I keep sub-folders out of the inbox. (I do not know if other considerations are important in gmail.)

Are you using "Favorite folders" in addition to unified folders? And you have marked an inbox as a favorite? The more times you show a folder, the more times Thunderbird is going to tell you about new messages in that folder.

You may want to play with the options in View (menu) > Folders and see if a different layout works better for you, unless you are already familiar with the options.

If you move an unread message to the trash, Thunderbird still considers it an unread message? That does not happen in my system. I wonder if changing when Thunderbird considers messages read might help. Thunderbird settings > general > reading & display > "automatically mark messages as read".

When I move an unread message to the spam folder, Thunderbird does still consider it unread. But I must manually mark the message as unread before moving it to make that happen. if I select the message normally before moving it, Thunderbird considers it read because I have "automatically mark messages as read" set to "immediately on display".

I'm not certain about all the causes and factors in this issue. If you try some changes and then post more screen images, I or someone else may be able to help more.
